UChicago team wins $10 million Laude Institute grant to advance AI weather forecasting for low- and middle-income economies | University of Chicago News 
 UChicago team wins $10 million Laude Institute grant to advance AI weather forecasting for low- and middle-income economies
 By 
 Casey Keel
 Nov 10, 2026 
 For many of us, the biggest decision we make based on the weather forecast is whether to carry an umbrella that day. But for a small farmer in a tropical climate, a decision about when to plant based on when the rainy season will arrive can be a make-or-break moment.
 This type of decision is at the heart of a $10 million grant awarded by the Laude Institute to a University of Chicago team to build AI weather forecasting models and support a software platform for people who depend on them. 
 The grant builds on the success of two past seasons, when governments in South Asia and Africa have used AI forecasts developed with the UChicago team to give more than 50 million smallholder farmers vital information about when the rainy season will arrive. The Laude funding will make that process faster, simpler, and more accurate, and extend it to new regions and new weather phenomena.
 For example, a farmer whose livelihood depends on knowing when the monsoon season will begin must decide whether to plant now or wait.
 However, farmers in tropical regions have long had less accurate and less actionable forecasts. One factor is that wealthy nations have developed modern weather forecasting models primarily for mid-latitude climates, using dense observation networks and supercomputers that most agencies located in tropical climes lack. 
 And even these forecasts are typically built to predict general conditions—not the specific events, such as when the rains will arrive, that drive farmers' most important decisions.
 The UChicago team is led by scientific AI expert Prof. Rebecca Willett , the Worah Family Professor of Statistics and Computer Science in the Wallman Society of Fellows; AI for atmospheric physics expert Prof. Pedram Hassanzadeh , an associate professor in Geophysical Sciences ; platform scaling expert Prof. Ian Foster , the Arthur Holly Compton Distinguished Service Professor of Computer Science ; and development economics expert Prof. Michael Kremer, Nobel laureate and University Professor in Economics and the College and the Harris School of Public Policy , and Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics at the World Bank Group. 
 This team is working to close the gap between mid-latitude and tropical forecasting abilities through AI-powered systems that can work with sparse observational data and modest computing resources. 
 Working at the frontier of AI weather modeling, the group has developed methods that take the best existing AI and physics-based forecasts, blend them, and tune them to the specific human-centered decisions that farmers, health officials, and emergency managers actually face.
 Over the last six months, the UChicago team and collaborators have cut the time needed to benchmark and adapt forecasting models from four to five months of expert labor to a single day of expert review. 
 “The leading AI weather models are evaluated on whether they accurately predict global temperature and precipitation,” Willett said. “That’s useful if you’re a meteorologist. But it tells you almost nothing about whether a model will correctly predict monsoon onset for a farmer in West Java or a dangerous heat wave for a public health official in Addis Ababa.” 
 Instead, Willett said, “We built our platform around a different question: not ‘how accurate is the model’ but ‘does this forecast help a specific person make a better decision in a specific place.’”
 With Laude Institute support, the team will build new AI weather forecasting frameworks embedded in the UChicago–Laude AI Almanac: a free, open-source platform that will let any meteorological agency, government, or nonprofit generate, evaluate, and deploy AI weather forecasts tuned to their own geography, observations, decision needs, and knowledge of local weather dynamics. The system runs without requiring specialized technical expertise, supercomputing infrastructure, or dense observational networks.
 "This platform will significantly accelerate the translation of the AI-driven weather forecasting revolution into enhanced capabilities of the meteorological agencies that need it most, so they can give high-quality, actionable information to the people they serve," said Hassanzadeh.
 Scaling to hundreds of millions
 Early deployments have already shown what’s possible using AI weather forecasts. From 2024 to 2026, the UChicago Human-Centered Weather Forecasts initiative supported government agricultural ministries in producing AI weather forecasts that were sent via text message to tens of millions of farmers in Africa and South Asia. 
 Those AI forecasts correctly predicted an unusual stall in the seasonal rains, providing an early warning to farmers. Farmers who received the AI-powered forecast on their phones could make informed planting decisions, rather than planting too early and losing their crop. 
 xThe Laude grant will help turn this work into a global platform covering many kinds of weather and climate hazards. Development banks and philanthropies such as the OpenAI Foundation and the Gates Foundation are investing heavily in delivering accurate weather forecasts and decision-support tools to farmers, public health workers, and government officials in low- and middle-income countries, with a goal of reaching hundreds of millions of people within the next several years. 
 The UChicago team works closely with these organizations—as well as the Agricultural Innovation Mechanism for Scale (AIM for Scale) initiative, the nonprofit Precision Development , and the University of California, Berkeley—on forecast delivery. 
 The work supported by the Laude Institute will strengthen the computational backbone behind those efforts with new AI methods, trusted evaluation focused on local community needs, and a scalable, open platform that expands access and increases forecast reliability, without major investments in computing infrastructure or software development.
 The platform will support not only agriculture but also public health and warnings of compound climate extremes.
 “Reaching hundreds of millions of people requires infrastructure that can scale across countries, datasets, and weather hazards,” said Foster. “With Globus , a non-profit research data management platform, we have learned how to make large-scale research computing reliable and accessible. We will draw on that experience to help meteorological agencies adapt and deliver forecasts for their communities without having to build and maintain their own computing infrastructure.”
 A companion AIM for Scale training program, co-led by UChicago and the United Arab Emirates' Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, is already preparing government meteorologists from 14 countries to use these tools, with the goal of reaching 30 countries by 2027. 
 "If this works for weather, it is a model for AI for public health, for education, and for many other areas where the people who need these tools most cannot pay for them," said Kremer. "Philanthropy can step up where the market cannot. That is what makes this moment extraordinary."
 —A version of this article originally appeared on the UChicago Data Science Institute website.
